screens.title: Encryption for Data in Transit & Certificate Management
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on protecting data while it travels across networks. You will learn the role of SSL and TLS in web traffic, how AWS services like Application Load Balancers and AWS Certificate Manager simplify certificate lifecycle tasks, and when to use public versus private certificates. We will also cover hybrid connectivity: IPsec VPN tunnels for encryption over the internet, and how Direct Connect requires encryption layered on top when you need confidentiality. Finally, you'll see why client-side encryption is a last-mile defense for highly sensitive data and the operational risk of losing keys. As we proceed I will show concrete examples, like requesting an ACM public certificate, attaching it to an ALB, and testing HTTPS with a redirect from HTTP. You’ll learn common mistakes to avoid—expired certificates, mixed content, and trying to export public ACM certs. By the end you’ll understand not only the tools but the practical trade-offs so you can choose end-to-end encryption or ALB termination patterns that fit your architecture. Additionally, you will learn client-side encryption patterns that encrypt sensitive data before it leaves the client, and how to manage the associated keys securely. Each objective pairs a concrete skill with why it matters: for example, ALB termination offloads compute and simplifies certificate lifecycle while client-side encryption reduces trust in intermediaries. We will also surface common mistakes — expired certs, mixed content, weak ciphers, and attempting to export public ACM certs — and how to avoid them. These objectives prepare you to configure secure communication channels and to choose the right certificate approach for internal or public use.

screens.title: SSL/TLS: Purpose and practical effects
screens.narratorSegment: SSL and TLS are cryptographic protocols that protect data in transit by providing confidentiality, integrity, and optionally authentication. In practice, TLS encrypts the bytes exchanged between a client and server, preventing eavesdroppers from reading or altering messages. A common deployment pattern in AWS is to use an Application Load Balancer to terminate TLS for incoming web traffic: the client negotiates a secure channel with the ALB using an ACM-supplied certificate, and the ALB then either forwards decrypted traffic to backends or re-establishes a TLS session to the backend for end-to-end encryption. The trade-off is operational: terminating at the ALB simplifies certificate lifecycle and offloads C P U cost, while end-to-end encryption ensures backends never see plaintext. For example, a public web application often terminates TLS at an ALB to reduce load on EC2 instances. A misconception is assuming TLS termination at the ALB always means data is unprotected inside your VPC; you can re-encrypt to preserve confidentiality. Key takeaway: choose where to terminate based on threat model, performance, and operational simplicity. Which part of your application truly requires end-to-end encryption?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › SSL/TLS: Purpose
Definition

What SSL/TLS protects

TLS ensures data confidentiality, integrity, and authentication between endpoints using symmetric encryption negotiated via asymmetric keys. It prevents passive eavesdropping and many active tampering attacks.

Concrete example: A browser opens HTTPS to a domain; TLS encrypts requests and responses so network sniffers see only ciphertext.
Common misconception: TLS termination at a load balancer equals insecure backend traffic — not necessarily; you can re-encrypt to backends for end-to-end protection.
Why it matters: Protects user credentials, session cookies, and API payloads from network attackers.
Deployment Patterns
ALB Termination
ALB handles TLS using an ACM certificate; backends receive decrypted traffic unless re-encryption is configured.
End-to-End Encryption
ALB terminates and then establishes TLS to backend targets, preserving encryption across the entire path.
Key Takeaway

Decide on termination by balancing performance and the requirement that backends never see plaintext.

screens.title: Application Load Balancer + ACM integration
screens.narratorSegment: Application Load Balancers integrate directly with AWS Certificate Manager to simplify TLS configuration. When you request an ACM public certificate and it is issued, you can select it as the default SSL certificate for an ALB HTTPS listener. The ALB then performs TLS termination, offloading cryptographic work from your application instances. After termination you have two common options: send decrypted HTTP traffic to backends if they are in a private, trusted network, or configure the ALB to re-encrypt to the backend by using certificates trusted by the backend targets. A concrete example: request an ACM public certificate for yourdomain. com, wait for issued status, then create an HTTPS listener on port 443 and choose the ACM certificate as the listener certificate. A common mistake is forgetting security group rules — ensure the ALB allows inbound 443 and that instances allow inbound from the ALB’s security group. Another pitfall is assuming you can export a public ACM certificate for use on an EC2 instance; public ACM certs cannot be exported. When you need certificates outside integrated services, request a certificate from a CA or use ACM Private CA for internal issuance. How will you configure backend encryption in your architecture?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › ALB + ACM Integration
Architecture

TLS termination with ALB and certificate association

Attach an issued ACM certificate to an ALB HTTPS listener to enable TLS for your domain. ALB handles TLS handshakes and can offload CPU from application servers.

Remember to configure security groups: ALB must allow inbound on 443 and target instances must accept traffic from the ALB security group.

Example workflow
Issue ACM cert → Create ALB → Add HTTPS listener port 443 → Choose certificate from ACM → Configure target group.
Pitfall
Public ACM certificates cannot be exported for use outside integrated services. Use ACM Private CA or an external CA for non-integrated servers.
Diagram (abstract)
Client ↔ ALB (ACM cert) — TLS
ALB ↔ Backend — HTTP or TLS depending on re-encryption
Key Takeaway

Using ACM with ALB simplifies TLS; decide whether backends should receive plaintext or TLS based on trust and compliance.

screens.title: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) — public vs private
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Certificate Manager streamlines provisioning and renewing certificates for use with integrated AWS services. For public certificates, ACM requests a certificate from a public CA, manages domain validation via DNS or email, and automatically renews and deploys certificates to services like ALB or CloudFront. You do not manage private keys or certificate files for ACM public certificates, and importantly, these public certificates cannot be exported. If you need certificates for internal microservices, devices, or servers that are not integrated with ACM, ACM Private Certificate Authority provides a private CA you control and can use to issue private certificates trusted inside your organization. Use a private CA when you need an internal trust chain and certificates that can be distributed to internal systems. A common misconception is that ACM public certs can be exported for on-premise use; they cannot. If you need exportable certificates for external systems, create a CSR with a traditional CA or use ACM Private CA with an appropriate distribution method. The operational advantage of ACM is less certificate maintenance and fewer manual renewals, which reduces expiry-related outages.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › ACM: Public vs Private
Definition

ACM responsibilities and limits

ACM public certificates: issuance from a public CA, automated renewal, domain validation, and deployment to integrated AWS services. Private CA: create your own CA hierarchy for internal trust and certificate issuance.

Example: Use ACM public cert for CloudFront distribution to serve HTTPS for a custom domain.
Misconception: Public ACM certs are exportable — they are not. For external, non-integrated uses, request a certificate using a CSR from a public CA or use Private CA.
When to use Private CA
  • Internal microservices that require mutual TLS and are not public-facing.
  • IoT devices or internal servers that require a private trust chain.
  • When you need the ability to export or distribute private certificates under your own control.
Key Takeaway

ACM reduces operational burden for public TLS; choose Private CA when you must run an internal PKI and issue certificates under your trust chain.

screens.title: Domain validation and certificate issuance in ACM
screens.narratorSegment: Requesting a public certificate in ACM follows a clear process: choose to request a public certificate, list the domain names and optional wildcard names, and select a validation method — DNS validation is recommended for automation. After you submit the request, ACM provides validation records or emails depending on the method. For DNS validation, ACM supplies CNAME records you add to your DNS provider; if you use Route 53 and the domain is managed there, you can choose to have ACM create those records automatically. Once the validation completes the certificate status changes to issued, and it becomes available to attach to services like ALB or CloudFront. A concrete example: request a certificate for yourdomain. com and *. yourdomain. com, choose DNS validation, and have ACM create records in Route 53. A common mistake is not waiting for the certificate to become issued before associating it with a listener, leading to configuration errors. Also, incorrectly created DNS CNAME records or failing to add the right records causes validation failures. Key operational note: after issuance, ACM handles automatic renewals for public certs — reduce expiry outages by relying on ACM where possible. What verification step will you automate in your environment?

keyIdea.text: Request public certs, validate via DNS (recommended), and attach the issued cert to AWS services. Automate Route 53 record creation when possible to avoid validation delays.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › ACM Issuance Process
Step-by-step
1. Request a public certificate
Add domain names and optional wildcards.
2. Choose validation method
DNS (recommended) or email validation.
3. Add validation records
Let ACM create Route 53 records or add CNAMEs manually.
4. Wait for status 'Issued'
Attach certificate to AWS services when issued.
Practical tips

Use DNS validation and Route 53 automation to avoid manual DNS errors. Confirm TTL and propagation. If validation fails, check the exact CNAME values and ensure no conflicting records exist.

Example: ACM provides a CNAME for _abcde.yourdomain.com pointing to a CA validation target — create that exact record.
Key Takeaway

Automate validation through Route 53 when possible to speed issuance and reduce manual errors.

screens.title: AWS VPN and Site-to-Site IPsec
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Site-to-Site VPN provides IPsec-encrypted tunnels between your on-premises network and an Amazon VPC. It uses standardized cryptographic protocols to protect confidentiality and integrity across the public internet. In a typical setup you configure a virtual private gateway or a transit gateway on the AWS side and a compatible VPN appliance on your side. The VPN negotiates IPsec tunnels and encrypts all traffic traversing those tunnels, so applications and services can communicate securely without exposing plaintext over the internet. A concrete example: connect your data center network to a VPC network range and route application traffic through the IPsec tunnel; traffic is then encrypted with strong ciphers. A common misconception is that VPN always provides the same performance and latency as Direct Connect — it does not. VPN runs over the public internet and is subject to variable latency and throughput. Key operational reminders: monitor tunnel health, ensure correct route propagation, and plan for redundancy. How would you design redundancy for encrypted hybrid connectivity in your environment? AWS VPN and Site-to-Site IPsec means use site-to-site vpn to encrypt traffic to aws; design for redundancy and monitor tunnel health because internet performance varies.. In practical terms, encrypting hybrid connections over the public internet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › AWS VPN (IPsec)
Architecture

Site-to-Site IPsec VPN

VPN creates encrypted tunnels from your on-premises gateway to AWS, protecting all traffic across the public internet. The AWS side typically terminates at a virtual private gateway or transit gateway.

Example: Corporate datacenter ↔ IPsec tunnel ↔ VPC; routing configured to send application subnets through the tunnel.
Misconception: VPN equals predictable performance — it does not; expect variable latency and throughput due to traversing the public internet.
Operational checklist
  • Configure strong cipher suites and lifetime settings for IPsec.
  • Monitor VPN tunnel health and automate failover to a secondary tunnel.
  • Ensure correct security group and route table settings to accept tunneled traffic.
Key Takeaway

Use Site-to-Site VPN to protect hybrid traffic over the internet. Plan for redundancy and monitor the tunnel for availability and performance.

screens.title: AWS Direct Connect and encryption choices
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated, private network connection between your premises and AWS, which reduces latency and increases bandwidth predictability compared to VPN over the internet. However, Direct Connect does not inherently encrypt traffic; the physical path is private but the data could still be exposed if network equipment or configuration is compromised. To ensure confidentiality, you typically layer IPsec VPN on top of Direct Connect. That creates an encrypted tunnel that travels over the private Direct Connect link and gives you both performance and encryption. A concrete example: use Direct Connect for high-throughput database replication and run IPsec tunnels between your on-premises gateway and a virtual private gateway to encrypt the replication traffic. A common misconception is thinking Direct Connect alone replaces encryption — it does not. In practice, combine Direct Connect for performance and IPsec for confidentiality when regulations or risk models demand encrypted traffic. Operationally, plan for routing and key management for the layered VPN, and test failover scenarios for both the physical and tunnel-level connectivity. What workload in your environment needs both the speed of Direct Connect and the privacy of IPsec?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Direct Connect & Encryption
Comparison

Direct Connect vs VPN

Direct Connect
Dedicated private line, predictable throughput, lower latency. Does not provide encryption by default.
Site-to-Site VPN
Runs over the internet with IPsec encryption. Subject to variable network performance.
Hybrid approach

When you need both performance and confidentiality, layer IPsec VPN over Direct Connect. This gives you a dedicated path with encrypted payloads. Ensure routing and keys are managed and monitor both physical connectivity and tunnel state.

Key Takeaway

Direct Connect provides performance; add IPsec if your threat model requires encryption across the private link.

screens.title: Client-side encryption: purpose and responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: Client-side encryption encrypts data on the client before transmission so the data remains encrypted in transit and at rest unless the recipient has the decryption key. This approach reduces trust in intermediaries, including cloud providers, because AWS sees only ciphertext. A concrete example from the source: use the S3 Encryption Client in AWS SDKs to encrypt objects locally with a client-side master key — possibly a KMS-managed CMK or a local key — before uploading to S3. The major operational responsibility is key management: you must protect and rotate the client-side master key. A safety-critical risk is losing that master key; if you do, the encrypted data becomes unrecoverable. A common misconception is thinking client-side encryption replaces the need for TLS — it does not. TLS still protects the encrypted payload during transmission against tampering and replay attacks. Use client-side encryption when you need to ensure that data is unreadable to intermediaries and you accept responsibility for key lifecycle. Ask yourself: do you have a reliable key backup and rotation plan if you adopt client-side encryption? Client-side encryption: purpose and responsibilities means encrypt sensitive data at the source, but manage keys carefully — losing the master key means losing access to the data.. In practical terms, encrypting data before it leaves the client and the risk of key loss. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Concept

Encrypt before you send

Client-side encryption means the client encrypts objects before upload, so intermediaries never see plaintext. Management of keys, rotation, and backups is your responsibility.

Risk: Losing the master key leads to unrecoverable data.
Code example (illustrative)

const encrypted = encryptWithKey(envelopeKey, plaintextData);

screens.title: Common mistakes in certificate management
screens.narratorSegment: Certificate management mistakes are common but avoidable with good monitoring and automation. The typical issues include expired certificates, incorrect domain validation, mixed content on secure pages, and weak cipher suite configuration. Expired certificates cause service outages and browser warnings; the remedy is automated renewal — ACM public certificates renew automatically, which greatly reduces this risk. Incorrect domain validation happens when DNS CNAME records are wrong or missing; ensure your DNS entries match the validation records exactly and automate with Route 53 where possible. Mixed content occurs when an HTTPS page loads resources over HTTP, causing browser warnings and potential blocking; always serve all assets over HTTPS and enforce HTTPS redirects. Weak cipher suites leave connections vulnerable; configure load balancers and web servers to use modern, strong TLS cipher suites. Another operational mistake is attempting to export public ACM certificates for external use — public ACM certs are not exportable, so plan certificate distribution accordingly. Detect issues by monitoring certificate expiry dates, scanning pages for mixed content, and testing TLS configuration with secure-cipher checks. In this chapter we focus on protecting data while it travels across networks. You will learn the role of SSL and TLS in web traffic, how AWS services like Application Load Balancers and AWS Certificate Manager simplify certificate lifecycle tasks, and when to use public versus private certificates. We will also cover hybrid connectivity: IPsec VPN tunnels for encryption over the internet, and how Direct Connect requires encryption layered on top when you need confidentiality. Finally, you'll see why client-side encryption is a last-mile defense for highly sensitive data and the operational risk of losing keys. As we proceed I will show concrete examples, like requesting an ACM public certificate, attaching it to an ALB, and testing HTTPS with a redirect from HTTP. You’ll learn common mistakes to avoid—expired certificates, mixed content, and trying to export public ACM certs. By the end you’ll understand not only the tools but the practical trade-offs so you can choose end-to-end encryption or ALB termination patterns that fit your architecture. What one encryption decision will you need to revisit in your current environment?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement SSL/TLS for web traffic using Application Load Balancers and managed certificates, provision and manage both public and private certificates with AWS Certificate Manager, and attach certificates to services like CloudFront and A P I Gateway. You will also configure encrypted hybrid links: establish IPsec Site-to-Site VPN tunnels for internet connectivity and layer IPsec over Direct Connect when you need privacy plus performance. Additionally, you will learn client-side encryption patterns that encrypt sensitive data before it leaves the client, and how to manage the associated keys securely. Each objective pairs a concrete skill with why it matters: for example, ALB termination offloads compute and simplifies certificate lifecycle while client-side encryption reduces trust in intermediaries. We will also surface common mistakes — expired certs, mixed content, weak ciphers, and attempting to export public ACM certs — and how to avoid them. These objectives prepare you to configure secure communication channels and to choose the right certificate approach for internal or public use.

Beyond configuration steps, competence here means making the right architectural decisions: choosing ALB termination when you want to offload TLS, or preserving end-to-end encryption when backends must never see plaintext. It means verifying domain validation processes, automating renewals, and knowing that public ACM certificates cannot be exported for on-prem use. It also means knowing when to create a private CA to issue internal certificates for microservices and IoT devices, and how to layer IPsec for hybrid connectivity over Direct Connect. You will practice a hands-on activity: request a public ACM certificate with DNS validation, attach it to an ALB listener, enable an HTTP to HTTPS redirect, and verify the padlock in a browser. For client-side encryption, you will examine how SDK-side encryption protects data before transmission and why losing the master key leads to unrecoverable data. These practical outcomes ensure you can both implement and defend your encryption choices during design reviews and incident responses.

SSL and TLS are cryptographic protocols that protect data in transit by providing confidentiality, integrity, and optionally authentication. In practice, TLS encrypts the bytes exchanged between a client and server, preventing eavesdroppers from reading or altering messages. A common deployment pattern in AWS is to use an Application Load Balancer to terminate TLS for incoming web traffic: the client negotiates a secure channel with the ALB using an ACM-supplied certificate, and the ALB then either forwards decrypted traffic to backends or re-establishes a TLS session to the backend for end-to-end encryption. The trade-off is operational: terminating at the ALB simplifies certificate lifecycle and offloads C P U cost, while end-to-end encryption ensures backends never see plaintext. For example, a public web application often terminates TLS at an ALB to reduce load on EC2 instances. A misconception is assuming TLS termination at the ALB always means data is unprotected inside your VPC; you can re-encrypt to preserve confidentiality. Key takeaway: choose where to terminate based on threat model, performance, and operational simplicity. Which part of your application truly requires end-to-end encryption?

Application Load Balancers integrate directly with AWS Certificate Manager to simplify TLS configuration. When you request an ACM public certificate and it is issued, you can select it as the default SSL certificate for an ALB HTTPS listener. The ALB then performs TLS termination, offloading cryptographic work from your application instances. After termination you have two common options: send decrypted HTTP traffic to backends if they are in a private, trusted network, or configure the ALB to re-encrypt to the backend by using certificates trusted by the backend targets. A concrete example: request an ACM public certificate for yourdomain. com, wait for issued status, then create an HTTPS listener on port 443 and choose the ACM certificate as the listener certificate. A common mistake is forgetting security group rules — ensure the ALB allows inbound 443 and that instances allow inbound from the ALB’s security group. Another pitfall is assuming you can export a public ACM certificate for use on an EC2 instance; public ACM certs cannot be exported. When you need certificates outside integrated services, request a certificate from a CA or use ACM Private CA for internal issuance. How will you configure backend encryption in your architecture?

AWS Certificate Manager streamlines provisioning and renewing certificates for use with integrated AWS services. For public certificates, ACM requests a certificate from a public CA, manages domain validation via DNS or email, and automatically renews and deploys certificates to services like ALB or CloudFront. You do not manage private keys or certificate files for ACM public certificates, and importantly, these public certificates cannot be exported. If you need certificates for internal microservices, devices, or servers that are not integrated with ACM, ACM Private Certificate Authority provides a private CA you control and can use to issue private certificates trusted inside your organization. Use a private CA when you need an internal trust chain and certificates that can be distributed to internal systems. A common misconception is that ACM public certs can be exported for on-premise use; they cannot. If you need exportable certificates for external systems, create a CSR with a traditional CA or use ACM Private CA with an appropriate distribution method. The operational advantage of ACM is less certificate maintenance and fewer manual renewals, which reduces expiry-related outages.

It uses standardized cryptographic protocols to protect confidentiality and integrity across the public internet. In a typical setup you configure a virtual private gateway or a transit gateway on the AWS side and a compatible VPN appliance on your side. Let's summarize the core concepts you should remember. First, SSL/TLS provides confidentiality and integrity for data in transit; the choice of where to terminate TLS affects both performance and privacy. Second, AWS Certificate Manager automates issuance and renewal for public certificates, and ACM Private CA enables an internal PKI for private certificates. Third, hybrid connectivity requires careful thought: Site-to-Site VPN uses IPsec to encrypt internet links, while Direct Connect gives predictable performance but needs an IPsec overlay if you require encryption. Fourth, client-side encryption protects data before it leaves the client, but you shoulder key management responsibilities, and losing keys makes data unrecoverable. Finally, avoid common mistakes like expired certs, mixed content, wrong domain validation, and weak ciphers. Keep these three concise reminders handy as you design secure communication channels. First, decide where to terminate TLS: ALB termination simplifies operations but re-encrypt to backends when needed. Second, rely on ACM for automating public certificate lifecycle and use ACM Private CA for internal certificate issuance — do not expect public ACM certs to be exportable. Third, secure hybrid links properly: Site-to-Site VPN encrypts internet links with IPsec, and Direct Connect must be combined with IPsec for confidentiality. Also remember client-side encryption is powerful but shifts key responsibility to you. Use automation and monitoring to prevent expiry, and always avoid mixed content.
